title: Satellite study finds villages cleared and river diversion under way at China's Medog dam site
dek: An Indian geospatial firm's analysis of imagery from Tibet says work on the 60 GW project upstream of Arunachal Pradesh has moved from clearing land to diverting the river. China still shares no river data with India.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Construction of China's 60-gigawatt hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo, the river that becomes the Siang and then the Brahmaputra in India, has moved from clearing land to diverting the river at its main dam site, according to an analysis of satellite imagery by an Indian geospatial company, reported on Monday and Tuesday.

The 18-page report, "Building at the Great Bend: Monitoring China's 60 GW Medog Dam Project", by EarthSense Labs, a firm incubated at IIT Delhi, compares images of the planned dam site near Mainling taken on 11 July 2025, 4 December 2025 and 10 August 2026. Villages and farmland visible on the south bank in July 2025 had been cleared by December, when earthwork had begun. By August 2026 the images showed river diversion works, extensive excavation, new roads, temporary housing and office buildings, the report says. The findings have not been independently verified, and neither government has commented on them.

## What the imagery shows

The report identifies work at several places along the river's Great Bend, where it drops more than 2,000 metres over about 50 km before turning south towards India. Besides Mainling, it marks a possible lower dam site near Pai town, where it found no conclusive sign of dam structures in imagery up to October 2026; a tunnel route under the Namcha Barwa massif; and a tunnel outlet and construction zone downstream near Medog, close to the Line of Actual Control. Work at the tunnel outlet began before the project's official ground-breaking, the report says. Imagery of the Medog area shows a bridge completed in 2021, 30 to 35 new residential and industrial buildings between 2023 and 2024, and a concrete batching plant built on former forest land between April and August 2024.

The company warns that the timing of reservoir filling and of water releases for power generation could change the Siang's flow, especially in the dry season, and alter how much sediment reaches the Brahmaputra floodplains in Assam and Bangladesh. The scale of any effect depends on storage capacity and operating rules that China has not published.

## Background

Premier Li Qiang announced the start of construction in July 2025. The project is planned as a cascade of five power stations, with an estimated investment of 1.2 trillion yuan (about $168 billion), using about 40 km of tunnels. Its planned capacity is about three times that of the Three Gorges Dam. The dam sites lie about 40 to 50 km north of Arunachal Pradesh.

China's foreign ministry has said the project has undergone "rigorous scientific research" and "will not adversely impact the water resources, ecology, or geology" of downstream areas, and that it is a matter within China's sovereignty. India's external affairs ministry has said it has conveyed its concerns as a downstream state and asked for transparency and consultation.

## The risk for India

India has no water-sharing treaty with China, and no data. Under memorandums first signed in 2002, China supplied flood-season readings from Tibetan gauging stations; the Brahmaputra memorandum expired in 2023 and has not been renewed, and India's Jal Shakti ministry says China has shared no hydrological data since 2022. On Monday, by contrast, China's foreign ministry spokesperson told reporters that Beijing would support Nepal's flood reconstruction with "ongoing sharing of weather, hydrological, and geological data".

India's answer is the 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, with a planned reservoir of about 9.2 billion cubic metres, which Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu says would let India absorb sudden releases from upstream and keep water flowing in the lean season. It faces opposition from Adi communities over displacement and land loss; protests in Pasighat turned violent on 23 October.

For Bengal and Bangladesh, the Brahmaputra, called the Jamuna in Bangladesh, is the second great river after the Ganges, whose sharing treaty with India expires on 12 December.

July 2025: construction formally launched; satellite imagery on 11 July shows villages and farmland at the Mainling dam site. 4 December 2025: settlements cleared, earthwork begun. 10 August 2026: river diversion works, roads, housing and offices visible. October 2026: no conclusive dam structures yet at the possible Pai site. Key figures: 60 GW, five stations, 1.2 trillion yuan (about $168 billion), sites 40-50 km from Arunachal Pradesh.
